critique.good: The identifying columns have useful space, United States stays on one line, and the score headings and values scan cleanly. The two-line rank heading uses the available header height well.
critique.problems: Both United Kingdom entries wrap, and the longer university names wrap; Cambridge also breaks across two lines. The alternating row heights make the rhythm uneven, though each row remains clear.
critique.cause: Country is 116px wide, leaving 95px for text, less than the 111px needed for United Kingdom. University is 190px wide, leaving 169px for names.

critique.good: The wider university column keeps Cambridge on one line and gives the long institute names more natural breaks. Score columns remain compact and easy to compare.
critique.problems: Every country wraps, making all seven data rows tall and leaving substantial empty space alongside short names and values.
critique.cause: Country is only 82px wide, leaving 61px for text. The extra 34px allocated to University comes at the expense of country names.

critique.good: The score columns have generous, fairly consistent spacing, and their headings stay intact. University names remain readable at word boundaries.
critique.problems: Every country wraps, creating tall rows and a large amount of empty space around the short scores. The wider score columns add little to the comparison while compressing the identifying columns.
critique.cause: Country is 82px wide, while the score columns have been expanded to 96, 98, 96 and 85px. University remains at 190px, so it retains the same name wraps as r0A.

critique.good: The four score columns form a clear, evenly spaced group, and each university name stays within two lines. The uniform row heights give the table a steady rhythm.
critique.problems: Every country wraps, making all seven rows tall and leaving substantial empty space beneath most names and scores. The repeated two-line countries draw attention away from the comparisons.
critique.cause: Country is 111px wide, leaving 90px for text; both country names need more space to fit on one line.

critique.good: Single-line country names make most rows compact. The score headings stay intact, the numerical columns align consistently, and the rules keep wrapped university names associated with their scores.
critique.problems: The Massachusetts name occupies three lines, creating one conspicuously tall row; Cambridge and California also wrap. The varying row heights interrupt the rhythm somewhat.
critique.cause: University is 174px wide, leaving 153px for text. Giving it more space would require narrowing a column that is already at or near the width needed to keep its contents intact.

r0A.idea: Give countries room to stay on one line while allowing longer university names to wrap and keeping the score columns compact.

r0B.idea: Favor university names with a wider first column, accepting two-line countries where needed.

r0C.idea: Give the score columns more breathing room for comparison, with university names and countries sharing the resulting taller rows.

r1A.idea: Move 5px from Country to University. This tests whether a little more room improves name breaks while United States still fits; United Kingdom will continue to wrap.

r1B.idea: Give Country the 132px needed for United Kingdom on one line, taking 16px from University. This tests a different balance: consistent, intact country labels in exchange for more wrapping in university names.

contrast.idea: The university column is too narrow for the primary row identifiers, forcing long names across several lines, while the score columns receive more space than their short values and headers need.

understanding.purpose: Compare the top seven universities by overall rank, country and four performance scores.
understanding.reading: Readers can find a university or rank, then scan across its row and down the score columns to compare institutions. Wrapped names and countries should remain clearly associated with their scores.
groups: University and Country identify each institution and provide context.
Teaching, Research, Citations and Industry are parallel numerical measures under the shared Score header; consistent spacing helps comparison.
Overall rank is the summary position for each institution.
keep_intact: Individual words in university names and countries
may_wrap: University names at word boundaries, particularly the longer institute names
Overall rank between its two words, using the two-row header height

bad.why: The university column is too narrow for the primary row identifiers, forcing long names across several lines, while the score columns receive more space than their short values and headers need.

contrast.why: The university column is too narrow for the primary row identifiers, forcing long names across several lines, while the score columns receive more space than their short values and headers need.

final.rationale: r0A gives the university names enough room to remain readable in at most two lines, while keeping the four score columns compact and similar in width. United States stays on one line, and the longer country name wraps naturally. The resulting mix of row heights follows the content without making every row as tall as the longest entries.

general: Give row identifiers enough width to preserve their readability, because readers use them to locate and compare records.
Columns with the same role benefit from a consistent visual rhythm, but their widths should also accommodate their headers.
Wrapping is acceptable when words remain intact and the row still reads as a unit.
specific: The four score columns need little space beyond their headers because their values are short.
Keeping United States on one line avoids adding a second line to five rows.
Overall rank can wrap in its header without disrupting the single-digit ranks beneath it.

final.tradeoffs: r0B gives university names more space and has regular row heights, but wraps every country name. r1B keeps both country names on one line, at the cost of a three-line university name and a noticeably taller row.
final.uncertain: The ranges are conservative visual estimates, not independently rendered thresholds. They describe one column varied at a time with the others adjusted proportionally to keep the total at or below 719px; their endpoints are not intended to be combined. Designers may reasonably prefer r0B's regular row rhythm or r1B's unbroken country names.

A.why: The score columns are compact and balanced, most country names stay on one line, and university names wrap without breaking words. Cambridge wraps, but the rows remain easy to scan.

B.why: The wider university column keeps Cambridge on one line and gives the long names clear two-line breaks. Every country wraps, making all rows taller, but the score columns remain well balanced.

C.why: The score group has a clear rhythm, but every country wraps and Cambridge also takes two lines. The wider score columns leave less space for the identifying text.

D.why: Every university name wraps, with the longest names taking three lines. The broad score columns have ample empty space while the row labels are compressed.

E.why: The score columns are compact and readable, but every country wraps and Cambridge takes two lines. The rank column has more space than its short values need.

F.why: The university column breaks Massachusetts and Technology within words, severely disrupting the row labels. Score columns and rank have generous space while several rows become very tall.

reviews.unsure: A and B make different reasonable tradeoffs: A keeps most countries on one line, while B gives university names more space but wraps every country.

A.why: The score columns are easy to compare and all words remain intact. Every country wraps, though, and Cambridge takes two lines despite unused space in the score columns.

B.why: The four score columns have a consistent rhythm and the university names are readable. Every country wraps, leaving many tall rows with empty space across the scores.

C.why: The score columns are balanced and their headers stay intact. Most countries and university names fit on one line, while longer names wrap cleanly, making the rows easy to scan.

D.why: Scores and headers are clear, but the narrow university column wraps every name, with the longest taking three lines. The wider score columns leave substantial empty space.

E.why: The university column breaks Massachusetts and Technology inside words, making key row identifiers difficult to read. Wide score columns leave considerable empty space beside those fragmented names.

F.why: The wider university column keeps five names on one line and wraps the longer two cleanly. Every country wraps, creating tall rows and a less compact comparison area.

reviews.unsure: F gives more room to university names, but C's mostly single-line countries and balanced score columns make its rows easier to scan overall.
